title: The Rabbit and the Tar Wolf
subtitle: A printed Cherokee animal story about a stolen drink

learningObjectives.text: What do the animals make to catch the water thief?

tarwolf.author: James Mooney
tarwolf.locator: Myth 21 · THE RABBIT AND THE TAR WOLF, normalized characters 451-1423
tarwolf.excerpt: They noticed that the Rabbit kept sleek and lively, although it was still dry weather and the water was getting low in the well. They said, "That tricky Rabbit steals our water at night," so they made a wolf of pine gum and tar and set it up by the well to scare the thief. That night the Rabbit came, as he had been coming every night, to drink enough to last him all next day. He saw the queer black thing by the well and said, "Who's there?" but the tar wolf said nothing. He came nearer, but the wolf never moved, so he grew braver and said, "Get out of my way or I'll strike you." Still the wolf never moved and the Rabbit came up and struck it with his paw, but the gum held his foot and it stuck fast. Now he was angry and said, "Let me go or I'll kick you." Still the wolf said nothing. Then the Rabbit struck again with his hind foot, so hard that it was caught in the gum and he could not move, and there he stuck until the animals came for water in the morning.

narrativeBlocks.body: The animals dig a well during a drought. They suspect Rabbit is secretly drinking from it at night.

narrativeBlocks.title: Rabbit gets stuck
narrativeBlocks.body: The animals make a wolf figure from pine gum and tar. Rabbit strikes it, becomes stuck, and is found the next morning.

narrativeBlocks.title: Mooney identifies a printed source
narrativeBlocks.body: Mooney's note attributes this version to the Cherokee Advocate of December 18, 1845. Treat it as a story preserved in a Cherokee newspaper, not as a direct transcript of a named oral performance.
